title: AN OLD WOMAN AND A VIRGIN WERE PREGNANT AT THE SAME TIME—And Luke Deliberately Brings Their Stories Together
paragraphs: AN OLD WOMAN AND A VIRGIN WERE PREGNANT AT THE SAME TIME—And Luke Deliberately Brings Their Stories Together

One woman thought her season had already passed. The other had barely entered hers. One pregnancy removed decades of disgrace. The other could expose a young woman to misunderstanding and shame. Then Luke brings them into the same room—and something happens before either child is even born that tells us exactly who Jesus is.
There is a moment in Luke 1 that is easy to read too quickly.
Don't.

Because if you slow down long enough to stand inside that little house in the hill country of Judah, you begin to realize that Luke has placed two women face-to-face who, humanly speaking, should never have been pregnant at the same time.
One was too old.
The other was a virgin.
Elizabeth had lived through years when pregnancy was expected but never came.
Mary became pregnant when pregnancy was not supposed to be possible at all.
One knew the ache of waiting.
The other was suddenly carrying a calling she could never adequately explain.
And somewhere between those two impossible pregnancies stands one staggering truth:
God is not imprisoned by the seasons that imprison us.
Maybe that is why this story still reaches into places we keep hidden.
Because some of us are Elizabeth.
We have prayed until the prayer became painful.
We watched other people receive what we begged God for.
We smiled at announcements that quietly broke our hearts.
We congratulated people while wondering, “Lord… when will it be my turn?”
And eventually we stopped asking out loud.
Not necessarily because we stopped believing in God.
Sometimes because hoping started hurting too much.
Then some of us are Mary.
God has allowed something into our lives that we cannot explain to everybody.
Something costly.
Something that makes obedience look frightening from the outside.
Something that leaves us wondering whether people will misunderstand us before they ever understand what God is doing.
Elizabeth represents the prayer that seemed too late.
Mary represents the calling that seemed impossible.
And Luke brings them together.
But before their meeting, he makes sure we understand something.

Elizabeth and her husband Zechariah were not introduced as rebels being punished by God. Luke describes them as righteous before God, walking faithfully in His commandments, and then immediately tells us that they had no child.
That matters.
Because suffering is not always proof that somebody has secretly failed God.
Sometimes faithful people wait.
Sometimes righteous people cry.
Sometimes people who love God carry questions they cannot answer.
Elizabeth had carried one of those questions for years.
Then Gabriel appeared to Zechariah.
The old prayer had been heard.
Elizabeth conceived.
And suddenly the woman who had probably watched the calendar betray her year after year was carrying a son.
Not merely any son.
John.
The forerunner.
The voice who would prepare the way of the Lord.
But six months into Elizabeth's miracle, Gabriel was sent somewhere else.
Not to Jerusalem.
Not to a palace.
Not to the daughter of a king.
Nazareth.
To a virgin named Mary.
Luke uses the Greek word παρθένος — parthenos.
Virgin.
He is not vague about it.
Mary herself asks the obvious question:
“Πῶς ἔσται τοῦτο…?”
Pōs estai touto?
“How will this be?”
Her question is understandable because what Gabriel has announced cannot be accomplished by ordinary human generation.
The answer takes us directly to God.
The Holy Spirit will come upon her. The power of the Most High will overshadow her. The child to be born will be holy and called the Son of God.
Then Gabriel gives Mary something astonishing.
Elizabeth.
The young virgin is told about the old woman.
The impossible calling is pointed toward the impossible pregnancy.
And then comes the declaration hanging over everything that follows:
ὅτι οὐκ ἀδυνατήσει παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πᾶν ῥῆμα
The heart of it is unmistakable:
No word from God will be impossible.
God points Mary toward Elizabeth as living evidence that human limitation does not have the final word when God has spoken.
But notice something beautiful.
Mary still has to respond.
And she does.
Ἰδοὺ ἡ δούλη κυρίου
“Behold, the servant of the Lord.”
Then:
γένοιτό μοι κατὰ τὸ ῥῆμά σου
“Let it be to me according to your word.”
That is faith.
Not pretending there will be no consequences.
Not knowing how every conversation will go.
Not receiving a ten-page explanation of the future.
Surrender.
Mary essentially places her life underneath the word of God.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to stop here.
Because you keep asking God to explain everything before you obey anything.
You want the entire road illuminated before taking the first step.
Mary did not receive that.
She received a word.
And she surrendered.
Then Luke does something cinematic.
Mary gets up.
Ἀναστᾶσα δὲ Μαριὰμ…
“Mary arose…”
She travels into the hill country “with haste.”
Picture it.
A young woman carrying a secret almost nobody could understand is traveling toward an older woman carrying a miracle almost nobody expected.
One womb carries the prophet who will announce the Messiah.
The other carries the Messiah Himself.
John and Jesus have not preached a sermon.
Neither has performed a public ministry.
Neither has been born.
Yet redemptive history is already moving.
Mary enters Zechariah's house.
She greets Elizabeth.
And suddenly Elizabeth's unborn child leaps in her womb.
Luke writes:
ἐσκίρτησεν τὸ βρέφος ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ αὐτῆς
“The baby leaped in her womb.”
Elizabeth is filled with the Holy Spirit.
And then she cries out.
Not quietly.
Luke describes a great cry.
“Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!”
Then Elizabeth says something so enormous that we should never hurry past it:
καὶ πόθεν μοι τοῦτο ἵνα ἔλθῃ ἡ μήτηρ τοῦ κυρίου μου πρὸς ἐμέ;
“And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”
My Lord.
τοῦ κυρίου μου — tou kyriou mou.
Elizabeth's miracle recognizes Mary's Lord.
That is the center of the scene.
John is extraordinary.
Elizabeth's pregnancy is miraculous.
But neither Elizabeth nor John is the center.
Jesus is.
That is what biblical Christianity keeps doing.
It keeps bringing us back to Jesus.
Not merely to miracles.
Not merely to blessings.
Not merely to answered prayer.
Not merely to inspirational stories.
Christ.
Elizabeth had received something she had wanted for years, yet when Mary walked through the door Elizabeth did not make the moment about herself.
Think about that.
She could have said, “Mary, look what finally happened to me!”
Instead, filled with the Holy Spirit, she recognizes what God is doing through someone else.
That kind of humility is rare.
Especially when we have waited a long time for our own miracle.
Sometimes we finally receive something from God and immediately make ourselves the center of the testimony.
Elizabeth doesn't.
Her miracle bows before the Messiah.
And John does something similar before he can even speak.
The forerunner's entire life will eventually carry one message:
Someone greater is coming.
Years later John will say of Christ:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
But Luke has already shown us the direction of John's ministry before John takes his first breath.
The messenger exists for the Messiah.
And then Elizabeth turns to Mary and says:
μακαρία ἡ πιστεύσασα
“Blessed is she who believed.”
Not blessed is she who understood everything.
Not blessed is she who controlled everything.
Not blessed is she whose obedience was guaranteed to be comfortable.
Blessed is she who believed.
Someone reading this has been trying to understand before surrendering.
You keep saying:
“God, show me how.”
“Show me when.”
“Show me why.”
“Show me what everybody will think.”
“Show me how this ends.”
And perhaps the question beneath all those questions is much simpler:
Will you trust Christ when obedience costs you control?
Mary believed.
Then she sang.
And her song—the Magnificat—is not sentimental decoration around Christmas.
It is saturated with the language, theology, memory, and hope of Israel's Scriptures.
Mary declares:
Μεγαλύνει ἡ ψυχή μου τὸν κύριον
“My soul magnifies the Lord.”
And:
ἠγαλλίασεν τὸ πνεῦμά μου ἐπὶ τῷ θεῷ τῷ σωτῆρί μου
“My spirit rejoiced in God my Savior.”
Do not miss those last words.
God my Savior.
Mary understood herself as someone who needed God's saving mercy.
Her song is not ultimately about Mary's greatness.
It is about God's greatness.
His mercy.
His holiness.
His strength.
His faithfulness.
His covenant promises.
His rescue.
She speaks of the proud being scattered, rulers being brought down, the humble being lifted, the hungry being filled, and Israel being helped according to God's mercy and His promise to Abraham.
The young woman carrying Jesus understands that what is happening inside her is bigger than her.
This is covenant history moving toward fulfillment.
The God who spoke to Abraham has not forgotten.
The God who made promises across generations has not misplaced them.
The silence between promise and fulfillment was never divine amnesia.
God remembered.
And perhaps that is where Luke 1 becomes painfully personal.
Because somebody reading this believes God has forgotten.
You have been Elizabeth for too long.
You prayed.
Waited.
Watched.
Cried.
Aged.
Adjusted.
Eventually you learned how to live around the empty space.
Or maybe you are Mary.
Something has happened that you never planned.
Your reputation feels fragile.
Your future feels uncertain.
You know what God has said, but you do not know how people will respond.
Or maybe you are Zechariah.
You prayed for something for so long that when the answer finally stood in front of you, unbelief had quietly replaced expectation.
That is one of the painful ironies of Luke 1.
Zechariah had apparently prayed for a child.
Then, when Gabriel announces the answer, Zechariah asks how he can know it is true.
Have you ever done that?
“God, please.”
“God, please.”
“God, please.”
Then God moves differently from what you imagined and suddenly:
“God… are You sure?”
We are complicated creatures.
We want miracles we can control.
Answers that arrive according to schedule.
Callings that never threaten our comfort.
Grace without surrender.
A Savior without lordship.
But Luke will not give us that Jesus.
The baby in Mary's womb is Lord.
And if Jesus is Lord, then Christianity cannot merely be something added to our existing life.
He comes to claim it.
That is where this beautiful pregnancy story becomes dangerous.
Because Jesus did not enter history merely to make December more sentimental.
He came because humanity needed saving.
The manger points toward the cross.
The child Mary carries will grow.
He will proclaim the kingdom of God.
He will touch the unclean.
Welcome sinners.
Confront hypocrisy.
Call people to repentance.
Forgive sins.
Give sight.
Raise the broken.
And eventually He will be rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
The Son Mary once carried will carry a cross.
The hands that once curled around His mother's finger will be pierced.
The One Elizabeth called “my Lord” before His birth will be crucified under the accusation of men.
And then—
the grave will lose.
Jesus Christ will rise.
This is why Christianity is not fundamentally advice about becoming a slightly better person.
It is news.
Good news.
The Gospel.
Christ died for our sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
And the risen Christ calls sinners to repent, believe, receive forgiveness, and follow Him.
Maybe that is the miracle you actually need.
Not merely for circumstances to change.
For you to change.
Because some of us have spent years asking Jesus to repair our lives while refusing to surrender our lives.
We want Him as rescuer when we are drowning but not Lord when He tells us where to walk.
We want grace without repentance.
Forgiveness without confession.
Resurrection without a cross.
But Jesus loves us too deeply to merely decorate the prison we refuse to leave.
He came to set captives free.
Maybe your scandal is not visible.
Maybe nobody knows.
The secret addiction.
The hidden messages.
The bitterness.
The pride.
The pornography.
The affair.
The dishonesty.
The resentment you have baptized as “discernment.”
The prayerlessness.
The double life.
The church face.
The private darkness.
The exhausting performance of appearing spiritually alive while something inside you is starving.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not pretending harder.
The answer is Jesus.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the grave.
Grace does not say your sin never mattered.
Grace says your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and His mercy is so great that your sin does not have to write your final chapter.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming darkness as light.
Not by telling sinners they were fine all along.
He rewrites lives through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation.
He takes guilty people and washes them.
Broken people and restores them.
Proud people and humbles them.
Ashamed people and covers them with grace.
Dead hearts and makes them alive.
And sometimes the first evidence that grace is rewriting you is painfully simple:
you stop hiding.
So be honest.
Did this expose something?
Did you recognize yourself somewhere between Elizabeth's waiting, Zechariah's doubt, Mary's surrender, and your own secret struggle?
And if Jesus has already taken a chapter of your life that looked ruined and turned it into a testimony of grace, tell us what He did.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to know that restoration is possible.
Your testimony may become another wounded person's reason to look toward Christ.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Because somebody on your Facebook friends list may be Elizabeth right now.
Somebody thinks it is too late.
Somebody is Mary, terrified by a future they did not expect.
Somebody is Zechariah, struggling to believe after years of disappointment.
Somebody looks perfectly fine in profile pictures and is privately falling apart.
Send it to someone.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, understand Christ more deeply, repent honestly, heal biblically, and keep walking when your faith feels weak, stay close.
We want this space to remain filled with Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, Gospel-centered healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment.
And for those who ask how they can help this work continue and expand, there is a practical way.
But I want to say this carefully because God's Word matters more than fundraising language:
The New Testament tells believers to give willingly, deliberately, generously, and “not reluctantly or under compulsion” because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
He will not.
It cannot.
Jesus purchased redemption.
Not us.
If this ministry has strengthened you, convicted you, encouraged you, or helped bring you closer to Scripture, prayerfully consider helping us keep doing it.
Not from guilt.
Not from pressure.
Not to earn God's favor.
But from willing partnership in spreading the Gospel and building resources that continually point people back to Jesus.
Do not leave this article merely impressed by Elizabeth.
Do not leave admiring Mary's courage.
Do not leave fascinated by Greek words.
Do not leave remembering Gospel Warrior.
Leave looking at Jesus.
Elizabeth eventually died.
Mary eventually died.
John eventually died.
Every ministry will someday end.
Every platform will disappear.
Every book will decay.
Every human voice will eventually become silent.
But Jesus Christ lives.
And Luke's story was leading us toward Him from the beginning.
An old woman carried the forerunner.
A virgin carried the Messiah.
The unborn prophet leaped.
Elizabeth cried out.
Mary worshiped.
And heaven was quietly announcing:
The Lord has come near.
The question now is not whether you find the story beautiful.
The question is whether the Lord of the story has your life.
Maybe you have wasted years.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe you have hidden sin.
Come into the light.
Maybe shame has convinced you that God could never want you again.
Look at the cross.
Maybe religion taught you how to appear clean while your heart remained far away.
Repent and come home.
Maybe you are tired.
Come to Christ.
Maybe you have fallen again.
Confess it.
Get up.
Run back.
Grace is not permission to remain in chains.
Grace is the pierced hand of Christ reaching into your darkness and calling you out.
So comment if you need prayer.
Share if someone needs hope.
But above everything else—
follow Jesus.
Because Elizabeth's impossible pregnancy was never the greatest miracle in Luke 1.
Neither was Mary's virgin conception presented merely as a spectacle of divine power.
The wonder is Who came.
God kept His promise.
The Savior entered our darkness.
The Lord came near.
And because He came, because He died, because He rose, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Remember this when shame starts reading your history back to you:
The scandal may explain where you have been—but only Jesus gets to decide what grace can make of what remains.
